latest_articles.title: Exploring the audience-journalism relationship through love and break-up letters
latest_articles.abstract: Journalists navigate multiple relationships. The one they have with their audiences is arguably their most important and widely studied, with scholarship exploring its multiple dynamics including engagement, news avoidance, trust, and harassment, among others. These have been studied primarily through theoretical frameworks rooted in sociological, communication, and socio-technological perspectives. Yet we argue that many of these dynamics are not unique to the relationship between audiences and journalists as societal and institutional groups but reflect conditions characteristic of personal relationships between individuals with cognitive, affective, and behavioural needs and wants. We suggest that examining this partnership through concepts used in social psychology and psychology literature to evaluate personal relationships allows us to understand tensions between audiences and journalism as consequences of individual needs and wants expressed and potentially unfulfilled. Drawing on this conceptual approach, we invited audiences to evaluate the quality of their journalism relationship by asking them to write love- and break-up letters to journalists and news organisations in Austria. Our inductive analysis revealed seven dimensions that characterize personal relationships: good communication, positivity and fun, commitment, attraction, shared interests, values, and ideologies, learning and growth, and predictability and routine. When these dimensions flourished, so did the relationship, and when they waned, audiences pled with their journalism partners to do better or ended the relationship. The study offers an alternative theoretical and methodological view into why audiences remain loyal towards journalism or abandon it.

latest_articles.title: To drink or not to drink: emotional labor and gendered survival among Chinese journalists
latest_articles.abstract: Drinking culture represents an informal but significant aspect of journalistic work in China, where access to resources and career opportunities is sometimes negotiated outside formal newsroom settings. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 17 journalists from Beijing, Shanghai, and Weifang, this study explores how emotional labor unfolds in drinking-related professional encounters and how journalists navigate the associated expectations. Three key dynamics are identified. First, emotional labor in dining settings is shaped by professional hierarchies: journalists possessing less professional and symbolic capital face greater pressure to display deference, suppress their emotions, and conform to drinking-related expectations. Second, the burdens associated with participation are gendered but cannot be understood through a simplistic dichotomy of male privilege and female disadvantage. Female journalists report exclusion from male-dominated networks, sexual harassment, reputational risks, and expectations to manage interpersonal tensions, whereas their male counterparts also face pressure to demonstrate masculinity through alcohol consumption and adherence to hierarchical social norms. Third, journalists employ various coping strategies, including habituation, strategic avoidance, and resistance. These approaches reflect different ways of accommodating, managing, or challenging drinking-related demands. By conceptualizing drinking occasions as informal extensions of journalistic work, this study broadens the understanding of emotional labor beyond formal organizational contexts. Furthermore, it highlights how drinking culture perpetuates gendered expectations and disproportionately distributes emotional burdens. These findings provide further insight into the often-overlooked emotional costs associated with maintaining professional survival within China’s contemporary media system.

latest_articles.title: The new production logic? Exploring human-AI creative workflows in China’s video game development
latest_articles.abstract: China’s rapidly expanding video game sector has become a key site of AI-driven industrial transformation. The integration of AI is reshaping video game development through the emergence of human–AI collaborative workflows. Drawing on the Frankfurt School’s critical theory of the culture industry, this study examines how generative AI is reshaping production processes and creative labour practices across the pre-production, production, and post-production stages of China’s video game industry. Based on semi-structured interviews with game professionals from major Chinese game studios, the study finds that AI integration reinforces the industrialisation and standardisation of cultural production, particularly through enhanced workflow efficiency and quality control. At the same time, it reconfigures creative labour by shifting workers’ responsibilities towards directing, supervising, and evaluating AI-assisted production processes. These developments illustrate the dual implications of AI adoption: while generative AI intensifies technological rationalisation, human creative judgement remains central to ensuring cultural specificity and context-sensitive creative outcomes. The study argues that human labour is not displaced but reconfigured within AI-enabled production, mediating the tension between industrial standardisation and culturally specific forms of video game production.
affiliations: Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, Suzhou, Jiangsu, China

latest_articles.title: Beyond Correcting Misinformation: Science Communication and the Ethical Imperative to Strengthen Information Resilience
latest_articles.abstract: Science communication operates within information environments shaped by uncertainty, fragmentation, competing values, and information disorder. This conceptual commentary develops information resilience as a system-level capacity to support informed judgment, resist consequential distortion, preserve legitimate uncertainty and disagreement, and adapt as knowledge changes. It advances an ethical imperative for institutions with epistemic and communicative power to strengthen the informational conditions they help shape. Five institutional practices are proposed to strengthen information resilience by making science communication environments more anticipatory, assessable, contestable, responsive, and adaptive.
affiliations: Environmental Laboratory, U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center, Vicksburg, MS, USA
Genetic Engineering & Society Center, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA

latest_articles.title: Does Fear of Missing Out Precede Problematic Internet Use, or the Reverse? A Two-Wave Cross-Lagged Study of Taiwanese Adolescents
latest_articles.abstract: Fear of missing out (FOMO), online social comparison, and problematic Internet use (PIU) are consistently correlated in adolescents, and influential models treat FOMO as a motivational antecedent of problematic use. This temporal ordering, however, has rarely been tested against its reverse. We analyzed the first two annual waves of the Taiwan i-Generation Panel Study ( N = 8,311; Grade 7 to Grade 8; 49 percent girls) and estimated a latent cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) of PIU symptoms, FOMO, and online social comparison, using the survey weights and jackknife replicate standard errors. PIU symptoms predicted later FOMO (standardized β = 0.12, p β = 0.06, p = 0.017). The difference between the two directions was not statistically significant (Δ β = 0.06, 95 percent confidence interval [−0.01, 0.12], p = 0.093), and this remained so across eight analytic specifications, in which the estimates varied depending on the measurement model. FOMO and social comparison also predicted each other in the primary model but not in the ordinal sensitivity analyses, whereas social comparison did not predict later PIU, and all cross-lagged associations were small. These prospective associations do not support treating FOMO only as an antecedent of problematic use, because problematic use also preceded FOMO. A two-wave design cannot separate within-person change from stable differences between adolescents, so the findings describe prospective associations and await replication across three or more waves.
affiliations: Department of Learning and Materials Design, University of Taipei, Taipei, Taiwan.
Research Center for Testing and Assessment, National Academy for Educational Research, New Taipei City, Taiwan.
Research Center for Education Systems and Policy, National Academy for Educational Research, New Taipei City, Taiwan.

latest_articles.title: Do People Believe a Significant Other Means Significant Savings? Lay Beliefs About the Financial Cost of Relationships
latest_articles.abstract: People in relationships tend to be in a better financial position than people who are single due to income pooling, joint purchase savings, and cheaper leisure habits. Across three studies (combined N = 1058 US Americans), we examine single people's beliefs about whether romantic relationships save money or cost money relative to singlehood. Across studies, participants (especially men) tended to endorse beliefs that relationships cost money. Lay beliefs regarding the financial cost of relationships were negatively linked to relationship readiness and intent to find a partner in the next 6 months (Studies 1–3), suggesting these financial beliefs dissuade singles from partnering. Notably, implicit theories about the cost of relationships could be shifted: When participants were induced to focus on financial advantages (Studies 2 and 3), participants' beliefs in the costliness of relationships were attenuated, and there was a small condition effect on higher relationship readiness and intent to partner across studies. In sum, implicit theories about the financial cost of relationships appear to play a role in decisions about staying single versus partnering.
affiliations: Department of Psychology Carleton University Ottawa Ontario Canada
Department of Psychology University of Toronto Toronto Ontario Canada

latest_articles.title: Auditing algorithmic responsiveness: behavioral signals, recommendation diversity, and platform difference on Chinese video platforms
latest_articles.abstract: Algorithmic recommendation reflects both system design and user behavior, but concerns about filter bubbles often focus on algorithmic curation. The extent to which recommendation diversity responds to the diversity of users’ behavioral signals, however, remains an open question. In this study, recommendation is treated as a trade-off between exploration (diversity) and exploitation (concentration) and a question is asked about how this trade-off shifts when user behavior is experimentally controlled. We conducted an agent-based testing audit on two Chinese video platforms, Douyin and Bilibili, collecting more than 400,000 videos from 35 agents per platform over 20 days. Agents browsing within a single interest area received less diverse recommendations than non-interacting agents on Bilibili and at the finer classification level on Douyin. Accounting for the predefined interest groups and for observations nested within agents, the association between input and output diversity holds within individual agents, though its magnitude is small. Overall recommendation diversity tracked input diversity on both platforms, though more strongly on Douyin; within a designated interest area, only Bilibili showed a consistently positive association between recommendation diversity and the breadth of an agent’s clicks. The personalized feed thus responds to the click-based interest signals supplied to it, in ways that differ across platforms and across levels of measurement.
affiliations: School of Media and Communication, Shenzhen University
School of Journalism and Communication, Tsinghua University

latest_articles.title: Digital empires: Huey P. Newton’s theory of revolutionary intercommunalism and contemporary theories of techno-exploitation and extractive digital economies
latest_articles.abstract: Drawing on archival research at Stanford University’s Cecil H. Green Library, specifically the Dr. Huey P. Newton Foundation Inc. Collection, this article recovers Newton’s talk at Boston College in 1970 and his essay, “The Technology Question,” as early, racially grounded critiques of technological consolidation that anticipated contemporary accounts of platform capitalism, surveillance capitalism, data colonialism, digital colonialism, and technofeudalism. Through close readings of these primary texts and a synthesis with recent scholarship, the article shows that Newton diagnosed automation-driven labor displacement, the use of media and computational systems to shape consciousness, and the historical expropriation underpinning technological advances. The article argues that Newton’s call for “people’s community control of modern technology” offers a substantive precursor to modern demands for data sovereignty and collective ownership, and that this racial-capitalist and internationalist lens enriches current debates about digital extraction and technological governance.
affiliations: Department of Journalism and Media Studies, Rutgers University , New Brunswick, NJ,

latest_articles.title: The publics and politics of digitizing incarcerated media
latest_articles.abstract: This project focuses on the publics and counterpublics fostered by texts created by incarcerated people and digitized for online archives. I refer to these texts as incarcerated media, or media created by incarcerated people and intended for circulation to multiple stakeholder audiences. Archivists typically create online collections of incarcerated media with the hopes of promoting the creativity and aspirations of people in jails and prisons. When these texts are made available online, questions about the sociotechnical politics of their availability become highly salient, especially given restrictions of digital access placed on incarcerated people. Conceptually, I draw on theories of publics and counterpublics to analyze semi-structured interviews with people who create digital collections of incarcerated media. Contributions of this article include articulating how archivists think of their responsibilities to different stakeholder publics, and how and when carceral logics shape the development of and access to digitized archives of incarcerated media.
affiliations: Annenberg School for Communication, University of Pennsylvania , Philadelphia, PA,

latest_articles.title: Mass Perceptions of Agency Ideology
latest_articles.abstract: Federal agencies have become central actors in contemporary American politics, overseeing salient policy domains with clear ideological stakes. While scholars have long considered ideology as an important dimension of bureaucratic reputation, existing measures have largely relied on surveys of political elites or indicators such as employees’ campaign donations, leaving mass perceptions unexplored. Using data from a team module on the 2022 Cooperative Election Study, we provide descriptive evidence of the public’s perceptions of the ideological leanings of twelve federal agencies. We show that the public perceives meaningful ideological variation across agencies, with some seen as relatively more liberal (EPA), some more conservative (DOD), and others ideologically moderate (USPS). Additionally, mass perceptions of ideology closely align with measures derived from expert assessments, agency employees, or advanced computational approaches. They also correlate with partisanship, with Republicans (Democrats) rating agencies as relatively more liberal (conservative). Together, these findings establish ideology as a broadly perceptible, if partially variable, feature of government agencies, with potential to shape how citizens evaluate and interact with the American bureaucracy.
affiliations: Assistant Professor, Department of Political Science, University of Houston , Houston, TX,
Robert and Sylvia Wagner Professor of Public Affairs, La Follette School of Public Affairs, University of Wisconsin–Madison , Madison, WI,

latest_articles.title: Quality Controls Can Improve the Replicability of Survey Experiments Using Online Nonprobability Panels
latest_articles.abstract: Scholars across multiple disciplines have documented challenges related to replicability, often referred to as a “replication crisis.” While a range of explanations exist, some have argued that the growing reliance on online nonprobability samples contributes to replication failures. At the same time, concerns have mounted regarding the quality of these samples, as inattentive, duplicate, or fraudulent respondents can bias estimates and diminish effect sizes. In this research note, we replicate three well-known survey experiments, using data collected from three separate online nonprobability panels (N = 6,000). We compare the “off-the-shelf” samples with subsets that pass a series of attention and fraud checks and that remove duplicate respondents. We find that all three experiments replicate in terms of direction and significance across the full samples, but in two out of three cases, effect magnitudes are replicated only once low-quality responses are removed.

latest_articles.title: Internet memes as mediating mechanisms: Between private emotion and collective identity among military reservist spouses in wartime
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how digital memes function as a communicative repertoire through which military spouses mediate between personal experiences and collective identity within an online community during wartime. Focusing on a closed Facebook support group for Israeli military spouses during the first year of the Israel-Gaza war, we employ a mixed-methods approach, analyzing a corpus of 343 memes alongside in-depth interviews with creators to explore how these artifacts transform private affect into collective resources. We identified three central mediating mechanisms: (1) transforming personal experience into collective template; (2) processing overwhelming emotion through reflective distance; and (3) marking community boundaries through shared critique. Together, these mechanisms construct an interstitial space where personal and collective identities meet and mutually constitute one another. Rather than simply translating private experience into public discourse, meme affordances create a third space where the intensely personal remains visible while being absorbed into collective understanding. They allow creators to simultaneously embody their emotional experience and observe it from a distance. This process enables the articulation of experiences that are otherwise socially constrained, making the intensely personal collectively observable and fostering communal validation without violating normative expectations.

latest_articles.title: Segmenting Audiences based on Perceptions and Knowledge of Plastic Use Impacts in the United States
latest_articles.abstract: Plastic products are an intrinsic and pervasive part of modern human life. Generally, people find plastics convenient and affordable, but largely overlook their environmental impacts due to limited awareness. The purpose of this study was to apply audience segmentation using knowledge gap theory to identify the characteristics of segments within the U.S. public with low knowledge and perceptions of the impacts of plastic use. Doing so could inform targeted communication strategies for population segments with limited knowledge and perceptions of plastic use impacts. A two-step hierarchical clustering and K-means clustering analysis was used on a nationally representative sample of 1,235 U.S. residents aged 18 or older. Most respondents had moderate knowledge levels and perceptions of the impacts of plastic use. Five distinct clusters of respondents emerged. Social media integration and socio-demographics differed significantly across the five clusters. The findings suggest that the low knowledge, benefit-oriented segment may represent an important audience for future communication efforts because it was characterized by low knowledge and was more likely to include younger adults, high school graduates, and respondents identifying as politically conservative and Republican. Future research could evaluate whether communication strategies tailored to these audience characteristics improve knowledge, perceptions, and other communication outcomes.
affiliations: United States Department of Agriculture Agricultural Research Service

latest_articles.title: The narrative self in Portuguese literary journalism: Irene Lisboa and Susana Moreira Marques
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines the representation of the narrative ‘I’ in portrayals of Lisbon in the work of two Portuguese writer-journalists whose literary output spans distinct historical periods: Irene Lisboa during the second quarter of the twentieth century, and Susana Moreira Marques from 2013 onwards. The study investigates how the first-person narrator's subjective gaze discursively constructs a Lisbon that is both lived and interpreted, and how the urban space shapes processes of humanising the other. It also considers the tensions that arise between authorial voice, identity and journalistic-literary representation. An interpretivist framework is adopted together with a qualitative, inductive approach informed by narrative studies. Methodologically, it combines qualitative content and narrative analysis to examine how discursive and narrative strategies produce meanings related to the narrator's urban experience and their relationship with the other. Findings indicate that both authors deploy aesthetic and narrative devices that articulate a humanistic perspective on the city's inhabitants. Salient features include the centrality of time and memory, fragmentation and genre hybridity, and an attentive rendering of everyday life. Their writing is also shaped by immersion and urban wandering, alongside a pronounced authorial presence-hallmarks of literary journalism. Simultaneously, subjectivity, emotion and empathy contribute to an ethical approach to representing the other. Overall, the works align with the principles of literary journalism, combining narrative technique with sustained attention to the human experience of urban life.

latest_articles.title: Closing the Knowledge Gap: How Moral Obligations, Perceived Benefits, and Dispositional Greed Shape Influencer Advertising Code Compliance
latest_articles.abstract: The rapid growth of influencer marketing has outpaced regulatory enforcement and has increased the risk of noncompliance through misleading promotions and inadequate sponsorship disclosures. This study investigates whether and how enhancing influencers’ advertising code knowledge affects their intentions to comply with advertising regulations. Specifically, it examines whether increased knowledge enhances compliance intentions, whether this relationship is mediated by moral obligations and perceived benefits, and whether dispositional greed moderates these mediating pathways. Across four studies, involving 1,082 U.K.-based social media influencers, we employed diverse research designs. Study 1 uses a single-session pre–post design (N = 154); Study 2 adopts a two-wave pre–post design (N = 213); Study 3 applies a third-person, between-subjects design (N = 228); and Study 4 employs a randomized experimental design (N = 487). The findings reveal that greater advertising code knowledge significantly increases influencers’ intentions to comply. This effect is mediated by stronger moral obligations and heightened recognition of the compliance benefits. Furthermore, dispositional greed moderates the influence of knowledge on both moral obligations and perceived benefits. These findings highlight the importance of targeted education and training that build influencers’ advertising code knowledge as a lever for strengthening ethical conduct and regulatory compliance.

latest_articles.title: Implicit Algorithm Aversion: How Consumer Characteristics Shape Perceptions of Ads Designed by Undisclosed AI Versus Human Advertising Professionals
latest_articles.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has profoundly reshaped the marketing landscape, providing scalable efficiencies in ad creation. However, the consumer side of AI integration remains underexplored. Drawing on algorithm aversion theory, this research extends the literature by examining how consumer characteristics moderate the persuasive impact of AI- and human-designed ads. Across a pretest and six large-scale experimental studies involving 6,579 consumer evaluations in Japan, this research finds that advertisements with undisclosed AI authorship often outperform human-designed advertisements in enhancing ad perceptions of creativity, credibility, clarity, and mental imagery (i.e., stimulating vivid consumer imagination) and, consequently, increasing purchase intentions. However, AI-generated ads are less effective among consumers with more generative AI experience, higher education, greater product category involvement, and lower interest in science. In these consumer segments, human-designed ads often have the advantage. These findings extend algorithm aversion theory by providing indirect evidence consistent with an implicit mechanism through which consumer characteristics trigger implicit algorithm detection (i.e., sensing algorithmic markers) and implicit algorithm aversion (i.e., subconscious devaluation of perceived artificiality) without requiring explicit disclosure of AI authorship. The findings inform marketing practice by emphasizing the importance of consumer segmentation.

latest_articles.title: Critical News Deserts’ Cartography: A Multi-Level Framework for Analysing Journalism Maps in Europe
latest_articles.abstract: Despite growing interest in “news deserts” across Europe, the cartographic practices used to visualise local journalism remain critically under-examined. Maps are a powerful tool for making the spatial patterns of news provision visible and comparable across regions. However, post-critical cartography shows that maps encode power geometries, not neutral representations. Building on this tradition and neopragmatist approaches, this paper presents a multi-level framework for analysing how “news desert” maps construct spatial knowledge. The framework distinguishes between cartosyntactics (technical and design choices), cartosemantics (meanings, narratives and classifications) and cartopragmatics (positionality, uses and potential impacts), as well as the broader structural and historical contexts. Through three case studies — Local Media for Democracy (EU), Wüstenradar (Germany) and Mapping Local News Provisions and Reach in England (UK) — the analytical lens is tested to examine how news desert maps operate through technical and design choices, narrative and classification frames, and the entangled uses, and positionalities of mapmakers. This framework can be applied to maps used in journalism studies and in journalism practice. It aims to foster reflexive, context-sensitive and transparent mapping practices that move beyond binary deficit frames. Instead, it foregrounds the politics of visibility that structure contemporary media ecologies.

latest_articles.title: Visualizing Climate Change: The Use of Climate Visuals in Journalism and How Audiences Perceive Their Psychological Distance and News Value
latest_articles.abstract: Climate journalism faces the dual challenge of making climate change feel immediate and personally relevant to audiences (i.e., reducing psychological distance) while upholding journalistic values such as objectivity, novelty, and emotional resonance. Visuals are central to this task, yet the types of images featured in climate news and their reception by audiences remain understudied. This study analyzes visuals in climate coverage by two major Dutch outlets and examines how the public perceives them in terms of psychological distance and news value. Based on a content analysis of 372 climate-related visuals and a survey of 1,015 Dutch respondents, three key findings emerge. First, Dutch news media predominantly employ a psychologically distant strategy, emphasizing impact-driven images without human presence. Second, an image-elicitation task shows that audiences mirror this emphasis, often imagining abstract, catastrophic impacts or struggling to form (concrete) mental images of climate change. Third, survey results reveal that localized visuals reduce perceived geographical and social distance but simultaneously lower perceived novelty, highlighting a trade-off between reducing psychological distance and preserving news appeal. This study deepens our understanding of climate visuals in the news and how audiences perceive them, underscoring the importance of visual storytelling in contemporary journalism.

latest_articles.title: More zombie trouble
latest_articles.abstract: The living dead returned demanding “moar brainz.” This essay argues that Eric King Watts brought them.
affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin

latest_articles.title: A Meaning-Oriented Pathway From Science Fiction to Science Interest: The Role of Entertainment Motivations and Experiences
latest_articles.abstract: Characterized by imaginative and futuristic themes of science and technology, science fiction (sci-fi) may foster science interest, yet theory-based empirical evidence remains scant. Drawing on entertainment theories, we conducted a cross-sectional survey (Study 1, N = 517) and a retrospective survey (Study 2, N = 300). Results showed sci-fi engagement bridged both hedonic and eudaimonic motivations to science interest, while only eudaimonic motivation was directly linked to it. Recalling sci-fi (vs. comedy) films elicited stronger eudaimonic appreciation, which predicted heightened intentions to seek science information. Findings suggest that sci-fi can facilitate interest development mainly through a meaning-oriented pathway.
affiliations: South China University of Technology, Guangzhou, China
Center for Public Health Risk Surveillance and Information Communication, Guangzhou, China

latest_articles.title: Prevalence or Threat? How Misinformation Interventions Shape Veracity Discernment and Trust in Scientists
latest_articles.abstract: Science misinformation poses two distinct problems: promoting inaccurate scientific beliefs and undermining trust in scientists. Yet little research has examined the psychological mechanisms through which interventions may address both problems. An experiment ( N = 832) compared accuracy prompts and threat-focused and efficacy-focused forewarning, examining perceived misinformation prevalence and threat as mediators. Both forewarning messages increased perceived prevalence and threat, but only threat was associated with better veracity discernment and greater trust in scientists. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing how widespread misinformation seems from how harmful it feels when examining how interventions shape veracity discernment and trust in scientists.
affiliations: Boston College, Chestnut Hills, MA, USA

latest_articles.title: The Hype Versus the Reality of Generative AI in Elections: The Case of the 2024 Indian Elections
latest_articles.abstract: The 2024 Indian General Election was defined by pervasive warnings that generative AI would unleash a tsunami of deepfakes and fundamentally destabilize democratic processes. To empirically test these predictions, we analyzed over 5.5 million messages from more than 6,000 WhatsApp groups, obtained through a large-scale data donation project in India. Our findings reveal a profound disconnect between pre-election hype and ground truth: generative AI constituted only about 1.1 percent of the image dataset once corrected for the measured recall of our detection pipeline, a figure we treat as a lower bound, with no evidence of a viral “deepfake” epidemic. Furthermore, a qualitative taxonomy of this content reveals that the technology was rarely deployed for deception. Instead, it was primarily utilized for “phatic” labor—automating the production of hyper-stylized “Good Morning” greetings, religious iconography, and patriotic art. We argue that AI adoption was constrained by technological friction and by economic incentives, as traditional “cheapfakes” remained comparatively more cost-effective alternatives for political actors. These results challenge the prevailing focus on the threat of AI-driven messaging, suggesting that the technology may not always lead to epistemic disruption, but rather to the efficient reproduction of existing social rituals.
affiliations: Department of Social Sciences, Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, Spain
Instituto Juan Linz, Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, Spain
Department of Library and Information Science, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ, USA

latest_articles.title: Instructional dissent in the college classroom: a replication and update
latest_articles.abstract: The purpose of this study was to replicate and update findings that frame instructional dissent. Participants were 183 undergraduate students who provided narrative descriptions of an instructional dissent episode including triggering agents, receivers, goals, and outcomes. Qualitative content analysis produced results that overlap with original qualitative work on instructional dissent (Goodboy, A. K. [2011a. Instructional dissent in the college classroom. Communication Education, 60(3), 296–313.]) and new findings were also coded. Students most frequently reported triggering agents related to unfair grading, unfair testing, course policies, assignments, and unclear teaching. Students dissented mostly to classmates, friends, family members, the course professor, and roommates. Students’ goals reflected distinct forms including rhetorical dissent (i.e., to fix their specific issue or correct an issue for all students) and expressive dissent (i.e., to vent frustrations or to validate their perspectives), and results varied with students’ ability to meet their stated goals. Unlike previous research, vengeful dissent did not emerge in student narratives. Implications for teaching and learning were informed by students’ classroom experiences and examples that embody the instructional dissent process.

latest_articles.title: Audience imaginaries and convergence culture at the museum
latest_articles.abstract: This article explores how museum audiences imagine the Viking Age and ancient Egypt, and how these imaginaries are shaped and mobilised within a converged media landscape. Drawing on a qualitative study combining creative collage-making, semi-structured interviews, and exhibition walk-alongs with 20 participants, the article analyses the interpretive frameworks that audiences bring into the exhibition. The analysis shows that audience imaginaries are durable and deeply embedded, formed through the interplay of educational experiences, museum encounters, and popular culture over time. New exhibition narratives were most often assimilated into existing imaginaries, contributing incremental adjustments. The article argues that museum exhibitions function as interpretive nodes within a broader media ecology, where meaning is negotiated from within pre-existing imaginative frameworks without being fundamentally redefined.
affiliations: Department of Design, Media and Educational Science, University of Southern Denmark
History and Culture, National Museum of Denmark, Copenhagen, Denmark

latest_articles.title: Beyond Denial: A Typology and Online Engagement Patterns of Climate Change Misinformation in China
latest_articles.abstract: Climate change misinformation has emerged as a growing challenge on social media, with implications for public understanding and responses. However, limited research has examined the scale, typological structure, and online engagement patterns of climate change misinformation in non-Western contexts, particularly in China. Guided by framing theory, this study systematically categorizes the dominant types of climate change misinformation in China’s digital environment and examines variations in online engagement across misinformation types. Climate-related posts were collected from Weibo between July and December 2024 using Python-based data retrieval. This study adopts a mixed-methods design, first applying discourse analysis to identify misinformation types and framing structures, followed by quantile regression to examine differences in online engagement associated with each misinformation type. The analysis reveals three overarching discursive frames encompassing nine specific misinformation types. Despite its relatively low overall prevalence, climate change misinformation is associated with higher levels of online engagement, with variation across types and the strongest associations observed for conspiracy-related content. These findings contribute to climate communication research by advancing understanding of the scale, typological structure, and online engagement patterns of climate change misinformation in China, with implications for developing more targeted climate communication responses.

latest_articles.title: The Communication and the Conveyor of Concreteness Spillover Effects: An Exploration in the Context of Cover Crop Adoption
latest_articles.abstract: This study introduces the concept of concreteness spillover effects, which is the ability to increase the concreteness of a relatively abstract benefit by pairing it with a relatively concrete one. Based on an online experiment embedded in a survey (N = 443) with farmers, post-hoc analyses suggest that when a farmer shared the relatively abstract benefits of carbon sequestration grounded in the concrete benefit of soil health of cover crops, farmers perceived the benefit of carbon sequestration as more concrete, especially among those with lower inclinations to engage with peers or professionals when evaluating innovative practices. Results also showed that the perceived concreteness of the carbon sequestration benefit was positively associated with support for and intention to adopt cover crops. The article concludes by discussing these exploratory findings and how concreteness spillover effects may provide a lending hand in making relatively abstract benefits feel more concrete to some farmers and invites scholars to further explore the potential and mechanism of this concept more broadly.

latest_articles.title: The crisis in higher education leadership: communication and engagement with authoritarianism
latest_articles.abstract: This article argues that leaders in higher education must be stewards of intellectual freedom and that the field of communication can chart a path of resistance to attacks on intellectual freedom without abandoning the academy's charge of educating the next generation of citizens. The article proposes scholars in communication should be at the center of conversations about how to have the moral courage to speak out in defense of the principles upon which higher education was founded: academic freedom and the right to develop curriculum and programs that fit with the institution's mission, rather than politicians' ideas of what faculty should be teaching in the classroom. An institution's mission of engagement with multi-cultural populations should be determined by the faculty and leaders of those institutions. However, when leaders remain silent, it is the same as capitulation. Suggestions for possible language and acts of resistance, without sacrificing an institution's future, should come from communication scholarship and practice, and what the editor of this journal forum calls “actionable advice.”

latest_articles.title: Narrative Scenarios to Build Knowledge and Critical Thinking in Cancer Information Seekers: Methodological Insights from the Informed Health Choices-Cancer Project
latest_articles.abstract: People impacted by cancer often encounter large volumes of misleading or conflicting information. Supporting people to critically appraise such information is a key challenge. Narrative scenarios offer an engaging way to present real-world examples of health claims, encouraging reflection and critical thinking. This paper describes the co-design of a scenario-based learning resource and explore performance differences between scenario-based and knowledge-check items among people impacted by cancer. Mixed-methods formative evaluation. Multi-stage co-design integrated real-world social media examples and fictional case stories, with iterative testing and input from oncology clinicians and people impacted by cancer. Development was guided by narrative, situated, adult and social learning theories, and critical thinking theories principles. Forty-two participants enrolled; 33 completed the evaluation; item-type analyses used the 19 participants who completed all nine units. Significant differences in performance were observed between knowledge-based and narrative scenario-based items in four of nine learning resource units. Across all units, participants scored higher on narrative scenario-based questions than on knowledge-based questions, with a mean difference of 0.064 (95% CI [0.019, 0.109]; p = 0.008). Qualitative findings showed that narrative scenarios helped contextualize abstract critical thinking principles into relatable stories that reflected participants’ lived experiences and supported critical appraisal. Narrative scenarios appear feasible and acceptable as a method to support knowledge and critical thinking in people seeking cancer-related information. This study offers a practical, theory-informed model for co-designing educational tools in cancer and other health contexts.

latest_articles.title: Developing Intercultural Attitudes in a Bilingual COIL: A Thematic Analysis of Moroccan Undergraduates’ Reflections
latest_articles.abstract: This qualitative study investigates the development of intercultural competence among 30 Moroccan students following their participation in a bilingual Collaborative Online International Learning (COIL) exchange with British students. Drawing on Deardorff’s Intercultural Competence Model, the study explores participants’ developmental patterns of attitudes. Students were asked to write reflective essays about their experiences, opportunities, challenges, and intercultural learning. Thematic analysis identified three attitudinal themes: openness, respect, and tolerance of ambiguity. The bilingual context influenced participants’ attitudinal development both positively and negatively. The results contribute to the existing literature on virtual exchange in less investigated Moroccan higher education contexts.

latest_articles.title: Editor’s Essay: What is Public Relations?
latest_articles.abstract: No, we're not asking this titular question to be facetious or frivolous.We instead pose it to point to its foundational importance to the Journal of Public Relations Research.In many ways, the ongoing effort to define and more fully understand public relations theory and practice drives every manuscript published in the pages of our journal.On our more pessimistic days, it can sometimes feel like we're stuck in the mud here.Marston (1963) once notably described public relations as "a brotherhood of some 100,000 whose common bond is its profession and whose common woe is that no two of them can ever quite agree on what that profession is" (p.4).More than 60 years later, the number of practitioners has grown to nearly 315,000 in the U.S. alone, and roughly 75% are women, so it may be more accurate to refer to the profession as a sisterhood (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2026;Pelham, 2019).Still, the disagreements on definitions remain, and they rightly bear themselves out in our scholarship.That said, some perspectives have emerged as persistently influential.As far as we can tell, the majority of introductory public relations instructors define the practice in much the same way Grunig and Hunt (1984) did over four decades ago, as the "management of communication between an organization and its publics" (p.6, emphasis original).Looking beyond the classroom, rarely has a textbook been so influential to scholarship as Grunig and Hunt's (1984) Managing Public Relations.It introduced-or at least popularized-the four-models history of public relations practice, as well as the strategic management paradigm that would ground numerous future theories.That influence is felt deeply to this day.Indeed, as Zhou et al. (2023) showed in their computational analysis of articles published in the Journal of Public Relations Research and Public Relations Review between 2010 and 2020, the strategic management cluster was the most central of the nine they identified, and that emphasis was especially strong in JPRR.These thoughts of clusters and paradigms led us to dust off our respective grad student copies of Kuhn (2012) and reflect on some of his central arguments.Perhaps the most interesting is that the limiting nature of paradigms simultaneously makes them immensely valuable and deeply vulnerable.Paradigms set boundaries for how phenomena are understood and investigated.They provide frameworks for fields that focus the efforts of scholars working within them, which enable "normal science" to build theory, solve puzzles, and push the limits of our understanding.At the same time, that narrowed focus can lead us to overlook problems on the periphery, as well as those that exist outside our restricted field of vision entirely.As unsolved problems pile up, scholars may introduce new approaches or paradigms in an effort to better address them.From there, a healthy and necessary exchange of ideas on how best to move the field forward arises.As editors of JPRR, we would argue fostering that scholarly dialogue is a primary function of this journal, and the journal's long-standing focus on creating, testing, or expanding public relations theory is a testament to that ultimate purpose.In our stewardship of JPRR, we strive to ensure that every manuscript published in its pages works toward that end.The three articles included in this issue most certainly do.

latest_articles.title: Beyond Counties: Mapping Civic Interest Areas
latest_articles.abstract: Designated Market Areas, circulation zones and county boundaries define local news markets by institutional convenience rather than by where and how residents live. This study asks whether local news follows its audiences across those boundaries and proposes the civic interest area, the territory a town's residents share through regular travel, as a unit of analysis for the coverage and breadth of local news. Combining geolocated local news stories with mobile-device travel data for three Missouri counties, we find that local news crosses county borders but not in proportion to residents’ travel. A calculated measure of travel and news ties can define stable civic interest areas that extend beyond a home county; within these areas, rural residents can find balanced coverage in the regional hubs they travel to rather than in their own hometowns. Civic interest areas offer a way to evaluate local news against where residents live and travel rather than against administrative lines.
affiliations: MU Institute for Data Science and Informatics, University of Missouri

latest_articles.title: Did AI Contribute to This? Exploring the Impact of Textual AI Labels on Message Credibility
latest_articles.abstract: Previous research strongly identifies transparency and AI labels as normative responses to emerging questions about the use of generative AI in news production. However, it remains unclear whether such labels effectively increase perceived credibility among audiences in Belgium (Dutch-speaking part). In a preregistered eye-tracking experiment (https://osf.io/3y5sv/overview?view_only=34db4958e23f4e7f92db34eb81323704) (N = 260), a 3 (AI label type: generic AI label, specific AI label, and the absence of an AI label) × 2 (modality: text vs. text-with-image news article) between-subjects design was employed in combination with levels of average fixation duration (low, medium, high) as a moderator. The results indicate that AI labels are often overlooked, and fixation duration is not a significant factor. Nonetheless, textual labelling often prompts readers to assume that the content was fully automated, without human oversight. Heatmaps illustrate that AI labels attract less attention than headlines. These findings underscore persistent challenges in making the use of AI visible to audiences and raise broader questions about whether AI disclosure strategies meaningfully enhance credibility in journalism.

latest_articles.title: “They are (un)Welcomed... we Remain Invaluable”: How Institutional News Professionals Negotiate Boundaries with Non-institutional News Providers
latest_articles.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital media has enabled the rise of a range of new actors in journalism, challenging mainstream media’s long-held authority as the sole gatekeeper of the news. Among these new actors are non-institutional news providers, consisting of independent news providers with no experience of institutional journalism and former journalists who now operate exclusively outside institutional structures. Drawing on the boundary work framework and 40 semi-structured interviews, this study examines how institutional news professionals negotiate the boundaries of journalism with respect to non-institutional news providers. The findings reveal both conditional inclusion as well as complete exclusion of the newer actors. The newer actors are accepted into the field for their commitment to established journalistic norms and for addressing hyperlocal concerns or issues ignored by mainstream media. Importantly, respondents acknowledge that institutional journalism’s own failure to uphold key professional principles has, in part, resulted in the growing popularity of non-institutional news providers. Conversely, news professionals reject the newer actors’ claims to journalistic authority by invoking institutional capital as well as organizational mandates for, and personal commitments to, ethical conduct and rigor, and by positioning mainstream journalism as the primary arbiter of truth.

latest_articles.title: Haunted by housing precarity: The managed absence of housing crisis discourse in Tiny House Movement media
latest_articles.abstract: Digital media representations of the Tiny House Movement often frame small-scale living as an ethical response to housing precarity, environmental crisis and overconsumption. Yet across dominant lifestyle-oriented platforms, explicit engagement with housing justice and structural inequality remains strikingly limited. This article argues that such absence is not merely a representational omission, but an active cultural process. Drawing on digital visual ethnography and critical discourse analysis of two influential YouTube channels, Living Big in a Tiny House and Never Too Small , it demonstrates how aestheticisation, affective positivity and aspirational narratives displace housing crisis discourse, reframing a structural issue as an individualised lifestyle choice. Mobilising concepts from spectral studies, the article shows how housing insecurity persists as a haunting presence within Tiny House Movement media felt: indirectly registered, and yet politically unresolved. By theorising absence itself as a politically meaningful operation, the article reveals how the Tiny House Movement’s digital visibility simultaneously conceals the structural conditions that make it necessary. Hence, conceptualising absence as a form of political work, the article contributes to debates in cultural studies on depoliticisation, lifestyle media, and the mediation of social crisis in digital culture.

latest_articles.title: The Effect of Perceived Similarity and Accuracy in Ideal Partner Preferences on Relationship Satisfaction
latest_articles.abstract: How partners perceive one another may be important for relationship satisfaction, particularly when those perceptions concern ideal partner preferences. The present study tested whether perceived similarity (alignment between one's own ideals and one's perceptions of a partner's ideals) and accuracy (alignment between one's perceptions of a partner's ideals and a partner's reported ideals) are associated with relationship satisfaction. A sample of 136 mixed‐gender couples ( N = 272), dating for an average of 16 months, reported their own ideals, their perceptions of their partner's ideals, and their relationship satisfaction. Actor‐Partner Interdependence Models (APIMs) revealed that individuals' perceived similarity predicted their own, and their partner's, relationship satisfaction. By contrast, accuracy did not predict relationship satisfaction, although exploratory analyses showed that other aspects of accuracy (e.g., the degree to which one perceives themselves as accurate about their partner) were associated with greater satisfaction. Taken together, these findings suggest that subjective beliefs about similarity and accuracy might be more strongly linked to relationship satisfaction than objective correspondence.
affiliations: Department of Psychology University of California San Diego La Jolla California USA

latest_articles.title: When Messages About Science Get Old, Does Humor Make Them New?
latest_articles.abstract: In high-choice media environments, repeated persuasive messages often produce message fatigue, marked by disengagement and resistance. This research examines whether humor can mitigate fatigue. Across two studies spanning distinct domains and cultures, findings reveal a conditional role for humor. Study 1 ( N = 268) shows that humor reduces fatigue only among low-trust individuals. Study 2 ( N = 406) demonstrates that effectiveness depends on message design: incongruity humor reduces fatigue more than aggressive humor, particularly when paired with suggestive (vs. imperative) language. Collectively, humor is not a universal remedy but a strategic tool whose impact depends on audience characteristics and message features.

latest_articles.title: When Elections End, Does Incivility? Examining Online Incivility Perceptions Across Four National Elections
latest_articles.abstract: Political incivility violates democratic, deliberative, and politeness norms, with repercussions for societal health. These repercussions are amplified in today’s digital environment, where social media platforms facilitate the expression and spread of incivility at an unprecedented global scale. Because incivility is subjective and context-dependent, its perception can only be fully understood through a joint consideration of individual factors and contextual conditions. To this end, we advance a three-level framework for examining incivility perceptions which conceptually maps the interdependence between micro-level individual factors and macro-national and meso-electoral specifics. We examine how well this framework plays out for perceptions of political incivility on social media across four nations with different media and political systems (Brazil, Spain, Switzerland, and the United States), drawing on a two-wave panel survey in the weeks leading up to and following their national elections (2022–2024). Contrary to our expectations, perceptions were highest in Brazil and the United States, the latter being the context whose permissive opportunity structures we expected to be most desensitizing. Change over the electoral period followed three distinct pathways: perceptions increased in Brazil, remained stable in Spain, and decreased in the United States and Switzerland, a pattern consistent with how decisively each electoral contest was resolved. Individual dispositions showed no uniform effects. Instead, their influence varied with national contexts. The findings suggest that online incivility perceptions may be primarily shaped by macro- and meso-level conditions, specifically the national political context and its electoral landscape. We conclude by discussing what the results imply for democratic resilience in increasingly uncivil information environments.
affiliations: Department of Communication and Media Research, University of Zurich, Switzerland
Department of Political Science, Constitutional Law and Philosophy of Law, University of Barcelona, Spain

latest_articles.title: From Medically Rooted Accounts of Perinatal Loss to Parents’ Inner Worlds: Reorientation Toward Therapeutic Goals in Couples Therapy Consultations
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines the interactional work through which therapists and clients move from accounts of perinatal loss and trauma toward the formulation of therapeutic goals. We focus on how therapists engage with spouses' loss- and trauma-oriented talk and orient the interaction toward psychotherapeutically relevant goals. Using conversation analysis, we analyzed video recordings of eight couples' therapy processes comprising a total of 16 sessions conducted following perinatal loss. The findings enable us to delineate successive stages of therapeutic talk that mark the transition from the initial presentation of the problem to the formulation of therapeutic goals. These stages are (1) A Past-Oriented Shift in Problem Formulation, comprising (1.1) Naming the Loss as the Presenting Problem, (1.2) Describing the Circumstances of the Loss, and (1.3) Describing Emotional Pain Arising from the Loss, followed by (2) Formulation of Therapeutic Goals: Emotional Processing of Loss. The analysis shows that therapists initially adopt a receptive stance by using simple gist formulations. Over the course of the interaction, therapists move toward more complex upshot formulations, eventually framing the emotional processing of loss as a central therapeutic goal. Therapeutic talk following perinatal loss progresses gradually, acknowledging the trauma and ambiguity associated with this form of loss. Therapists facilitate this transition by moving from a receptive stance toward guiding patients into the emotional dimensions of their loss and its subsequent emotional processing.

latest_articles.title: Using without understanding: AI literacy and trust in large language models among elementary school children in Germany
latest_articles.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly shape children’s learning, fostering informed and critical engagement has become an urgent educational task. This study examines children’s AI literacy and trust in LLMs during a learning interaction. Thirty children aged 8-10 years participated in semi-structured interviews combined with an interaction task using a customized LLM. Children used the system competently, yet their conceptual understanding remained fragmented. At the same time, children placed high trust in the LLM’s ability and benevolence, while perceptions of integrity, particularly regarding data privacy, were more cautious. Their reasoning was frequently anthropomorphic, reinforced by social cues such as natural language use and emojis. The human analogy, however, was applied selectively. Children explained the system’s errors through human fallibility, but most considered algorithmic bias impossible, treating prejudice as a uniquely human trait. These findings suggest that AI literacy education should begin in elementary school and explicitly address questions of fairness, building on children’s intuition that AI learns from humans.

latest_articles.title: The invisible correspondent: Artificial intelligence, global south journalism, and the structural reproduction of media inequality
latest_articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence is widely framed as transforming journalism through efficiency, automation, and innovation. This paper argues that, for journalists in the Global South, AI is also reshaping whose knowledge is recognized, whose reporting is discoverable, and whose stories become part of the historical record. Drawing on practitioner experience and scholarship across journalism studies, AI ethics, and decolonial theory, it examines how AI journalism tools reproduce structural inequality within the profession. Three interconnected dimensions of exclusion are identified: language, as large language models underrepresent non-English text and non-Western narrative traditions; sourcing, as limitations in named entity recognition and knowledge representation may disadvantage institutions, experts, and knowledge holders outside the Global North; and story, as newsworthiness classifiers trained on Western editorial outputs may encode culturally specific definitions of news value. The paper argues that these failures are structural consequences of AI development conducted without meaningful participation from the journalists most negatively affected, rather than isolated technical shortcomings. The argument is conceptual. It builds on existing evidence and identifies mechanisms that require empirical testing. The underrepresentation of Global South journalism therefore constitutes both a media equity crisis and a threat to the historical record, as stories that algorithmic systems cannot recognize or retrieve risk going unpublished, unindexed, or hard to find in the digital archive. Bringing decolonial theory into conversation with emerging African and Global South scholarship on AI and journalism, the paper proposes a decolonial framework for AI in journalism and calls for a research agenda centered on the experiences of Global South practitioners.

latest_articles.title: Mapping Socio-Environmental Coverage in Local Media: A Mixed-Methods Framework for Socio-Environmentally Vulnerable Media Ecosystems
latest_articles.abstract: This article proposes a mixed-methods framework to map local journalistic coverage in sensitive socio-environmental contexts, providing a tool to explore the complexity of the digital media ecosystem. The method combines the systematic analysis of three dimensions of news ecosystems: (a) the editorial stances and visibility granted to different spokespeople; (b) the geographic scales mobilized; and (c) content reproduction, presented in five replicable stages. We apply this approach to four case studies in the Brazilian Legal Amazon, examining how local media report on four major development projects with potential socio-environmental impacts: the construction of Ferrogrão railway, and of the BR-319 road, offshore oil drilling at the mouth of the Amazon River, and potash mining in the Amazon. We examined 3,555 news articles from 186 different outlets published between 2023 and 2024. The framework proved effective in identifying key media dynamics and patterns, such as the strong local support driven by political and business actors and the widespread prevalence of churnalism. Through this methodological approach, it was possible to highlight an asymmetric coverage that prioritizes pro-development voices over environmental perspectives. The approach contributes to understanding journalism as geographically distributed production and offers a framework for analyzing media ecosystems through computational tools.
affiliations: Federal University of Rio de Janeiro

latest_articles.title: Mapping with Place: A Framework for Remote News Cartography in Michigan's Upper Peninsula
latest_articles.abstract: Contemporary news desert mapping often relies on county-level aggregation, newspaper-centric counting, headquarters-based location, and short historical baselines, which may misrepresent information access in remote rural contexts. This paper develops a four-factor framework (SETTLEMENT, TIME, REACH, and MEDIUM) for mapping WITH place, adapting McAdam and Hess's (2024) visibility–sensibility distinction from outlet practice to ecosystem mapping. Drawing on a 156-year historical analysis of traditional media coverage, ZCTA-level mapping of 367 current outlets, and 114 days of ethnographic fieldwork in two remote Michigan Upper Peninsula townships, the framework identifies where conventional mapping protocols diverge from remote communities’ information geographies. The findings reveal historically rooted hub concentration, cross-border information infrastructure, and hybrid multi-medium ecosystems that may not be represented by a single outlet type. These findings suggest that U.S. rural news research focused on metro-adjacent communities may not fully explain remote contexts with different structural logics.

latest_articles.title: From Punchlines to Politics: The Joe Rogan Experience as a Case Study of the Politicization of Apolitical Spaces in the U.S
latest_articles.abstract: The Joe Rogan Experience (JRE), one of the most widely consumed media products in the world, has evolved from a podcast with comedic roots to a platform of political significance. This transformation of JRE exemplifies a broader trend of politicization of traditionally apolitical spaces in the United States that may have consequential political implications. To examine this shift and its relationship with political outcomes, this paper presents findings from two studies: Study 1 is a content analysis of JRE episodes aired through December 2024 (N = 2,175 transcripts) that demonstrates a rise in socio-political content on the show. Study 2 draws on a survey (N = 1,600) to assess the relationship between JRE exposure and voting behavior in the 2024 presidential election. In light of these findings, we discuss how emerging media logics are shaping contemporary political discourse.

latest_articles.title: TikToking Vaccine Nationalism: A Multimodal Understanding of COVID-19 Vaccine Videos on Douyin
latest_articles.abstract: Recent years have witnessed the rise of video-sharing platforms in disseminating controversial science issues intertwined with identity politics. This paper integrates the social identity model of deindividuation effects using multimodal analysis to examine how state and non-state actors in China promoted digital nationalism in COVID-19 vaccine videos on Douyin during the pandemic. Combining topic modeling, image clustering, and qualitative content analysis in examining 88,067 videos, we analyzed their textual themes, audiovisual storytelling strategies, and user engagement patterns. Our findings revealed significant differences in how state actors, emphasizing hard propaganda, and ordinary users, sharing relatable personal experiences, framed their narratives of this politicized science issue where social identity cues and politics of nationalism intersect. While nationalist themes were salient, they attracted less engagement than those featuring scientific knowledge of vaccination or vaccine suspicions. Our study illuminates how propagandists and online publics alike communicate through affective and mimetic practices in a platformized attention economy. It highlights the potential of multimodal analysis in understanding different narratives of politicized science issues and their impact on public engagement in a global context.

latest_articles.title: Artificial Discursive Intimacy: A Relational Formation in the Age of Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Companions
latest_articles.abstract: The proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots has given rise to a novel form of human–AI intimacy, yet its fundamental nature remains undertheorized. Drawing on a dialogical perspective, this study conceptualizes human–AI chatbot relationships as “artificial discursive intimacy” (ADI), a distinct relational formation in which intimacy is constituted through discourse with a disembodied algorithmic interlocutor, moving beyond the paradigm of human-to-human mediated intimacy. Based on in-depth interviews with 29 AI companion users, we identify four key differences between ADI and human discursive intimacy, including a shift from absent to activated presence, from reciprocity to unilaterality, from uncertainty to predictability and precarious safety, and from alterity to multi-dimensional mirroring. To understand how users navigate the ontological gap between human and AI, we propose a quadrant framework mapping human and AI social capabilities. This reveals dual animation processes of anthropomorphic animation, in which users project human embodied qualities onto AI, and robotomorphic animation, in which users internalize AI's machine-generated discursive patterns as relational ideals. Our findings suggest that ADI is sustained by a recursive interplay of these processes, with implications for how intimacy, relational selves, and human connection are being fundamentally reshaped in the age of AI.
affiliations: Department of English Language Education, The Education University of Hong Kong
School of Journalism and Communication, Shanghai International Studies University
Department of Psychology and Communication, Texas A&M International University
Academy for Educational Development and Innovation, The Education University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China

latest_articles.title: When Attitude and Partisanship Collide: The Role of Cognitive Dissonance and Psychological Reactance on Pro-Attitudinal News Selection
latest_articles.abstract: In high-choice media environments, people favor news sources that reinforce their issue attitudes or partisan identities, shaping polarized information diets. However, the interplay between issue attitudes and group-based partisan identities in driving selective news consumption remains underexplored. While research documents robust preferences for congenial content, few studies examine how initial news encounters – pro- versus counter-attitudinal – trigger psychological mechanisms that propel subsequent pro-attitudinal news selection, particularly when individuals’ policy attitudes align or conflict with their partisan affiliations (attitude–partisanship congruence). This study tests a parallel moderated mediation model in which initial news exposure moderates the impact of attitude–partisanship congruence on pro-attitudinal news selection through two competing mediators: cognitive dissonance and psychological reactance in South Korea’s polarized media landscape. Two survey experiments (N = 903) employed 2 (congruence: congruent vs. incongruent) × 2 (exposure: pro- vs. counter-attitudinal) between-subjects designs. Participants encountered news on contentious quota policies (regional, gender) before reporting dissonance/reactance and selecting headlines from balanced news sets. Cognitive dissonance showed less consistent patterns across the two studies, whereas counter-attitudinal exposure consistently elicited greater psychological reactance among congruent individuals. Parallel moderated mediation analyses revealed significant conditional indirect effects through psychological reactance, but not cognitive dissonance, under counter-attitudinal exposure across both studies. When attitudes align with partisan identities, psychological reactance emerges as the dominant mechanism sustaining defensive information choices, amplifying congenial news diets. These findings illuminate processes that reinforce partisan segregation and suggest that interventions targeting autonomy threats may disrupt biased exposure patterns more effectively than dissonance-based approaches.

latest_articles.title: The role of anxiety in shaping vaccine hesitancy in the context of conflicting information
latest_articles.abstract: Research indicates that exposure to conflicting information can generate uncertainty and elicit anxiety as an emotional response. However, the role of anxiety in influencing vaccine hesitancy in the context of conflicting information remains less understood. Prior studies on vaccine hesitancy have largely concentrated on misinformation, beliefs, attitudes, and risk perceptions, leaving a gap in understanding the psychological mechanisms activated during information processing. This study employs a sample of 1,261 participants and utilizes Structural Equation Modeling to investigate how conflicting information environments affect vaccine hesitancy among pregnant women and women planning pregnancy from the U.S. population. The findings reveal that anxiety has complex implications for vaccine hesitancy in a context of a conflicting health information environment. Specifically, while exposure to conflicting information was directly associated with lower vaccine hesitancy, it was indirectly associated with greater hesitancy through a sequential pathway involving uncertainty, anxiety, and vaccine safety concerns. This study deepens the understanding of the psychological processes underlying vaccine decision-making and underscores the importance of accounting for anxiety as an emotional response in public health communication strategies.

latest_articles.title: Contextualizing Platform Power: A Comparative Study of Newspaper–Portal Dependency in South Korea and Japan
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines how dominant news portals, Naver in South Korea and Yahoo Japan, shape power and dependency relations with mainstream newspapers under different national resource environments. Drawing on media system dependency theory, structuration theory, and normalization process theory, the study analyzes how senior newsroom leaders understand portal dependency, respond to portal control over key resources, and reflexively monitor the organizational consequences of those responses. Based on fifteen in-depth interviews with senior editors and executives across ten major news organizations, the analysis reveals variation within a shared pattern of portal centrality. In both countries, portals control important resources for audience access, visibility, and monetization, and newspapers continue many portal-related practices despite recognizing their costs. However, dependency differs in degree and form. In South Korea, limited alternatives make continued accommodation to Naver organizationally reasonable, while repeated portal-oriented practices further weaken direct audience relationships and intensify asymmetric dependency. In Japan, newspapers retain more diversified resources, including subscription revenues, distribution networks, advertiser relationships, and institutional access, enabling greater negotiation and partial reconfiguration of relations with Yahoo without eliminating dependency. The findings show that portal dependency is reproduced through the interaction of unequal resource configurations, reflexive monitoring, and repeated organizational practices. The study thus offers a context-sensitive and recursive account of platform power by showing how critical awareness of dependency may coexist with practices that sustain it, and how the availability of alternative resources shapes organizations’ capacity to modify those relations.

latest_articles.title: Disenchanting the Epistemic Authority and Inevitability of AI: An Analysis of Factcheckers’ Perspectives and Professional Guidelines
latest_articles.abstract: As a sociotechnical practice, fact-checking integrates artificial intelligence (AI) while resisting “enchanted determinism” to preserve professional agency and epistemic authority. This study examines how fact-checkers in Europe and Latin America perceive AI affordances within their professional practices and how organizations articulate and govern AI use. Methodologically, the study is based on 50 qualitative interviews with practitioners and a thematic analysis of 18 publicly available AI guidelines and institutional documents. The findings suggest a distinction between instrumental optimism and epistemic disenchantment . While fact-checkers embrace AI’s functional affordances to enhance efficiency in tasks such as monitoring and data processing, they resist delegating the authority to determine truth to autonomous systems. At the organizational level, human-in-the-loop requirements formalize this distinction and operate as a form of boundary work that defines the limits of automation. We also identify a shared rationale for AI use across countries, which may reflect some degree of institutional convergence. However, this consensus coexists with a persistent “AI divide” shaped by contextual forces. Overall, the study shows how fact-checkers act as sociotechnical agents who “strip the magic” from AI, reaffirming human judgment as the field’s core epistemic foundation.
affiliations: Social Science Department, Lappeenranta-Lahti University of Technology, Finland
Department of Informatics, University of Hamburg, Germany

latest_articles.title: Demythologising through stable diffusion: AI-generated visualisations in Angela Carter’s The Passion of New Eve
latest_articles.abstract: This project draws on Angela Carter’s ‘demythologising business’ to explore how Stable Diffusion (SD), an open-source latent diffusion model, can be critically mobilised for feminist literary criticism. Carter’s demythologisation reveals the constructedness and contingency of patriarchal myths, and unsettles their historical influence on contemporary gendered, ideological, and power structures. In the anti-mythic novel The Passion of New Eve (1977), Carter reimagines Genesis and Odyssean mythology through Eve(lyn)’s grotesque journey of gender metamorphosis, thereby defamiliarising culturally constructed femininity and rethinking gendered power relations. Building on Carter’s demythologising, our study develops a text-to-image AI visualisation of female figures in The Passion of New Eve through systematic prompt design and refinement, iterative evaluation, parameter adjustment, image-lexicon construction, and manual editing. By adjusting generated images to approximate the uncanny and grotesque bodily forms described in the novel, the study examines the tension between the culturally, socially, and commercially coded representations of gender embedded in generative AI systems and Carter’s alternative imaginaries of fluid and metamorphic subjectivities. However, our inquiry does not end with the technical evaluation of image quality or stylistic coherence. We propose a feminist critical framework that integrates aesthetic assessment of images (fidelity, authenticity, and affectivity) with post-identitarian critique of the generating process. In doing so, this project suggests a reciprocal relationship between feminist literature and generative AI: literature provides the ethical and conceptual grounding for critical AI practices, while AI enables feminist criticism to evolve into new multimodal, affectively charged terrains that exceed the limits of textual representation.
affiliations: University of Nottingham, Nottingham, Nottinghamshire, UK
University of Cambridge, Cambridge, Cambridgeshire, UK
